text: Part 1: prime sums g; part 2: recursion S(v, j).

Min_25 sieve (Min_25 筛) computes Σi≤n f(i) for a multiplicative f in about O(n3/4 / log n), for n up to 10¹⁰–10¹¹, provided f(p) is a low-degree polynomial in p and f(pk) is easy. Part 1: for every value v = ⌊n/i⌋ compute g(v) = Σp≤v, p prime pe by a sieve that removes, prime by prime, the numbers whose smallest prime factor is that prime.

Part 1 transition for the j-th prime pj (only for v ≥ pj²): g(v) −= pje · (g(⌊v/pj⌋) − g(pj−1)). There are only 2√n distinct values ⌊n/i⌋, stored in two arrays indexed by v (small) or n/v (large). Start from g(v) = Σ2≤i≤v ie, as if every number were prime.

Part 2: S(v, j) = Σ f(i) over 2 ≤ i ≤ v whose smallest prime factor is ≥ pj. It is (the prime part) g-values minus the primes below pj, plus, for each prime pk ≥ pj with pk² ≤ v and each power pke: f(pke)·S(⌊v/pke⌋, k + 1) + f(pke+1). Answer = S(n, 1) + f(1), computed by plain recursion without memo.
For φ: f(p) = p − 1, so part 1 needs two sums: primes counted (e = 0) and primes summed (e = 1); f(pk) = pk−1(p − 1). P5325 has f(pk) = pk(pk − 1), which needs e = 1 and e = 2.

Prints π(n) (from part 1) and Σφ(i) for i ≤ n (part 2), both checked against a plain sieve in Python up to 10⁶. The sum of primes below each prime is recomputed in a loop here for clarity; in real use keep it as a prefix-sum array.

The values in g overflow fast: Σ i up to 10¹⁰ is 5·10¹⁹, beyond long long. Real problems work modulo a prime; with exact sums, keep n small enough or use __int128. Precompute the prefix sums of primes, or the inner loop costs an extra factor.
f = g * h; h lives on powerful numbers.

The Powerful Number sieve (PN 筛) sums a multiplicative f up to n when some easy multiplicative g agrees with f on primes, g(p) = f(p), and its prefix sums G are known. Write f = g * h (Dirichlet convolution). Then h(p) = 0, so h is nonzero only on powerful numbers (every prime exponent ≥ 2), and there are only O(√n) of them up to n.

Σi≤n f(i) = Σd powerful h(d) · G(⌊n/d⌋). Find h(pk) from f(pk) = Σi=0..k g(pi) h(pk−i), then DFS over primes ≤ √n with exponents ≥ 2. Below, f(pk) = k·pk with g = id, so G(m) = m(m+1)/2. When G itself needs a sieve (杜教筛 or Min_25), PN wraps around it.
Checked against a direct sieve of f up to n in Python. The work is the number of powerful numbers, O(√n), plus the cost of G; for n = 10¹⁰ it runs in milliseconds.

Key points to memorise
1. Values ⌊n/i⌋: 2√n of them; index small v directly, large by n/v.
2. Part 1: g(v) −= p^e (g(v/p) − g(p_prev)) for v ≥ p²; start as if all were prime.
3. Part 2: S(v, j) = primes ≥ p_j up to v + Σ f(p^e) S(v/p^e, k+1) + f(p^(e+1)).
4. Answer S(n, 1) + f(1); about O(n^(3/4) / log n).
5. PN: g(p) = f(p) ⇒ h = f / g is 0 off powerful numbers; Σ h(d) G(n/d).
